stem: Who was the Austrian chancellor whose system of censorship and repression collapsed in March 1848?

options.content: Metternich
options.rationale: Correct: he resigned and fled after the Vienna rising of 13 March 1848.

options.content: Schwarzenberg
options.rationale: Schwarzenberg became chief minister later, in November 1848, and restored Austrian power.

options.content: Radetzky
options.rationale: Radetzky was the Austrian general who commanded in northern Italy.

options.content: Kossuth
options.rationale: Kossuth was the leader of the Hungarian national movement, an opponent of Austria.

explanation: **Metternich** had dominated Austrian policy since 1815; the Vienna rising of 13 March 1848 forced him out.

stem: Which king of France abdicated in February 1848?

options.content: Louis Philippe
options.rationale: Correct: he abdicated on 24 February 1848 and a republic was proclaimed.

options.content: Charles X
options.rationale: Charles X was overthrown in the revolution of July 1830.

options.content: Napoleon III
options.rationale: Louis Napoleon was elected president in December 1848 and later became Emperor Napoleon III.

options.content: Louis XVIII
options.rationale: Louis XVIII was restored in 1814-15 and died in 1824.

explanation: The February Revolution in Paris brought down **Louis Philippe**, king since 1830.

stem: What did most liberals of the 1840s want?

options.content: The vote for every adult man and woman at once
options.rationale: Very few people demanded votes for women, and most liberals wanted a property qualification.

options.content: Abolition of all private property and of the monarchy
options.rationale: These were socialist or radical aims, not liberal ones.

options.content: A constitution and an elected parliament
options.rationale: Correct: they wanted government limited by law and by a parliament.

options.content: A return to the absolute monarchy of the eighteenth century
options.rationale: That was the conservative position that liberals opposed.

explanation: **Liberals** wanted constitutions, parliaments, the rule of law and freedoms such as a free press; most wanted the vote limited to men of property.

stem: Where did the first of the major risings of 1848 break out, on 12 January?

options.content: Paris, in France
options.rationale: The Paris revolution came in February 1848, after the rising in Sicily.

options.content: Palermo, in Sicily
options.rationale: Correct: the Sicilians rose against the King of the Two Sicilies about six weeks before Paris.

options.content: Vienna, in the Austrian Empire
options.rationale: Vienna rose on 13 March 1848.

options.content: Berlin, in the Kingdom of Prussia
options.rationale: Berlin rose on 18 March 1848.

explanation: Although Paris was the main trigger, **Palermo** rose first, on 12 January 1848.

stem: Which economic problem helped to cause the revolutions of 1848?

options.content: A sudden fall in food prices that ruined townspeople
options.rationale: Prices rose, not fell; it was townspeople who struggled to buy food.

options.content: The collapse of the Zollverein customs union in 1847
options.rationale: The Zollverein did not collapse; it continued to grow.

options.content: Poor harvests and high food prices in 1846-47
options.rationale: Correct: potato blight and a poor grain harvest drove up the price of food.

options.content: A shortage of workers that forced factories to close
options.rationale: The problem was unemployment, not a shortage of workers.

explanation: Potato blight from 1845 and the poor harvest of 1846 pushed up food prices, and the financial crisis of 1847 caused **unemployment**.

stem: Why was the Metternich system a cause of the revolutions of 1848?

options.content: It gave the vote to the middle class, which then demanded the overthrow of kings
options.rationale: Metternich's system gave no new rights to the middle class.

options.content: It blocked peaceful reform, so reformers felt only revolt could bring change
options.rationale: Correct: censorship and repression left no legal route to change.

options.content: It encouraged nationalism by creating a united Germany and a united Italy
options.rationale: The 1815 settlement kept Germany and Italy divided.

options.content: It made Austria an ally of the revolutionaries in France
options.rationale: Metternich opposed revolution everywhere.

explanation: By censoring opinion and crushing revolts, the system **blocked reform**, so pressure built up until it burst out in 1848.
hints: Think about what happens to demands for change when there is no legal way to express them.

stem: Which statement best explains why news from Paris in February 1848 led to risings elsewhere?

options.content: The new French republic sent its armies to start revolutions across the rest of Europe
options.rationale: The French provisional government did not invade other countries in 1848.

options.content: Louis Philippe fled to Vienna and called on Austrians to rise up
options.rationale: Louis Philippe went into exile in Britain.

options.content: It caused the potato blight to spread into the German states
options.rationale: The blight was a plant disease that began in 1845, not a result of politics.

options.content: It encouraged opponents of other governments and shook rulers' confidence
options.rationale: Correct: rulers remembered how revolution had spread from France in 1789.

explanation: The fall of the French king **encouraged reformers** and **frightened rulers**, many of whom gave way quickly.
hints: Think about the effect of the news on two groups: the reformers and the rulers.

stem: Which of these was a weakness shared by many of the revolutions of 1848?

options.content: They were all led by members of the old ruling families
options.rationale: The leaders were mostly middle-class liberals, not royal families.

options.content: They all broke out in countryside areas far from the capital cities
options.rationale: Most revolutions began in cities such as Paris, Vienna and Berlin.

options.content: None of them made any demands for a constitution or a parliament
options.rationale: Constitutions were among the most common demands.

options.content: Middle-class liberals and workers wanted different things
options.rationale: Correct: liberals wanted constitutions; workers wanted jobs and social reform.

explanation: The coalition of **liberals and workers** split once the first demands were met, which helped the old rulers recover.
hints: Who joined the crowds, and did they share the same aims?

stem: Britain did not have a revolution in 1848.
explanation: True. The Chartists held a mass meeting in London in April 1848, but there was no rising.

stem: The Congress of Vienna of 1815 created a united Italian state.
explanation: False. The settlement left Italy divided into several states, with Austria ruling Lombardy and Venetia.

stem: Match each term with its meaning.

right.content: Measures of 1819 that censored the press and controlled universities
Rule by a king or emperor with no constitution limiting his power
Government limited by a constitution and a parliament
The belief that a people sharing a language and culture should rule themselves

explanation: These four terms describe the ideas of 1848 and what they were directed against.

stem: Put these events in chronological order.

left.content: Metternich resigns after the rising in Vienna
Revolution in Paris replaces Charles X with Louis Philippe

explanation: 1830 revolution in Paris; Palermo (12 January 1848); Louis Philippe abdicates (24 February 1848); Metternich resigns (13 March 1848).
hints: One of these events happened in 1830.

explanation: The February Revolution in **Paris** triggered the wave of revolutions.

points.description: Aimed to preserve the 1815 settlement / the power of monarchs, especially in the Austrian Empire.
Censorship of the press and books / police spies.
Control of universities and student societies (Carlsbad Decrees, 1819).
Intervention by the great powers against revolutions (Naples and Piedmont 1821, central Italy 1831).

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Metternich, the Austrian chancellor, wanted to preserve the settlement of 1815 and the power of monarchs, because liberalism and nationalism threatened the multinational Austrian Empire. His system used censorship of newspapers and books and a network of police spies. The Carlsbad Decrees of 1819 placed German universities under supervision and banned student societies. The great powers were ready to intervene against revolutions, and Austrian troops crushed risings in Naples and Piedmont in 1821 and in central Italy in 1831.

stem: Explain why liberalism and nationalism had grown in influence by 1848.

points.description: Identifies the legacy of the French Revolution and Napoleon.
Explains that ideas of rights and the redrawing of borders showed change was possible.
Identifies the growth of the educated middle class / newspapers and Romanticism.
Explains that this class was shut out of power, so it demanded constitutions and national unity.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The French Revolution and Napoleon left a lasting legacy: people remembered ideas of citizens' rights and equality before the law, and Napoleon had swept away many small states, showing that borders could change. At the same time the educated middle class of lawyers, teachers and merchants grew. They read newspapers and Romantic writings about national languages and history, but they were shut out of power by absolute rulers, so they demanded constitutions and national unity.

hints: One reason looks back to 1789-1815; another looks at how society was changing.

stem: Explain why so many revolutions broke out in 1848.

points.description: Identifies long-term liberal and national demands.
Explains that the Metternich system blocked reform, so frustration built up.
Identifies the economic crisis of 1845-47.
Explains that high food prices and unemployment brought workers and artisans onto the streets.
Identifies the trigger of the February Revolution in Paris.
Explains that news spread quickly, encouraged reformers and made rulers give way.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Liberals and nationalists across Europe wanted constitutions and national self-government, but the Metternich system of censorship and intervention blocked any peaceful reform, so frustration built up for thirty years. The economic crisis of 1845-47 turned this into action: potato blight and a poor harvest raised food prices, and the financial crisis of 1847 caused unemployment, so hungry workers and artisans were ready to join liberal protests. The trigger was the fall of Louis Philippe in Paris in February 1848. News spread by railway and telegraph, encouraging reformers elsewhere and shaking rulers' confidence, so Vienna and Berlin rose within weeks and most rulers gave way.

hints: Long-term causes, short-term causes and a trigger.

stem:
Study the sources and answer the questions.

**Source A** — a letter by a fictional weaver in a Silesian village to his brother in America, written in February 1848 (invented for this question)

> Bread costs twice what it did two winters ago, and the merchant pays less for each piece of cloth because the factory looms work faster than we can. Three families in our street have nothing in the house. People no longer talk of the king with respect. If something does not change, I do not know what the young men will do.

**Source B** — a pamphlet by a fictional liberal lawyer in Vienna, printed secretly in 1847 (invented for this question)

> We are not children to be told what we may read. Every newspaper is cut by the censor's scissors, every lecture is watched by the police. A free people needs a constitution, a parliament and a free press. Until we have them, Austria will remain a prison of the mind.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: What does Source A suggest about the condition of workers in 1848?

points.description: They faced poverty / high food prices (bread twice the price).
They were losing work or income to factories / were losing respect for the king.

parts.explanation: Two inferences supported from the source.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: How far do Sources A and B agree about the causes of discontent before 1848?

points.description: Agree: both show discontent with the existing government / a demand for change.
Disagree: A stresses economic hardship (bread prices, factory competition).
Disagree: B stresses political grievances (censorship, police, no constitution).
Judgement: they agree that change is needed but show different causes (social and political).

parts.explanation: Points of agreement and disagreement, each supported.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: How useful is Source B as evidence about why revolution broke out in Vienna in March 1848? Use the source and your own knowledge.

points.description: Useful: shows liberal demands for a constitution, parliament and free press.
Useful: confirmed by own knowledge of censorship and police control under Metternich.
Provenance: written by a liberal lawyer, a member of the educated middle class that led the revolution; secret printing shows the strength of censorship.
Limitation: one-sided pamphlet meant to persuade; written in 1847, before the events.
Limitation: ignores economic causes (unemployment, food prices) and the trigger from Paris.
Supported judgement on usefulness.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Source B is useful because it shows the political grievances of the educated middle class who led the revolution in Vienna: anger at censorship and police spies, and demands for a constitution, a parliament and a free press. My own knowledge confirms that Metternich's system censored the press and watched the universities, and the fact that the pamphlet had to be printed secretly is itself evidence of censorship. However, it is a persuasive pamphlet by a liberal, so it exaggerates ('a prison of the mind'), and it was written in 1847, before the events. It also says nothing about the unemployment and high food prices that brought workers onto the streets, or about the news from Paris that triggered the rising on 13 March. It is useful for the political causes but gives only part of the explanation.

parts.explanation: Usefulness judged from content, provenance and own knowledge.

hints: Each source shows a different kind of grievance. Ask who wrote it and why.

parts.stem: Describe the revolution in Paris in February 1848.

points.description: Reformers held political banquets to demand a wider franchise; the government banned one.
Demonstrations turned into street fighting / barricades.
The National Guard would not defend the king.

parts.stem: How far was economic distress the main cause of the revolutions of 1848? Explain your answer.

Economic: financial crisis and unemployment (1847); artisans and peasants' grievances.
Other: liberal and national demands blocked by the Metternich system.
Other: the trigger of Paris and the loss of nerve by rulers; Palermo before Paris.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
Economic distress was very important. Potato blight from 1845 and the poor grain harvest of 1846 pushed food prices sharply higher, and the financial crisis of 1847 threw many people out of work. Artisans such as weavers were already losing work to factories, and peasants resented labour services. This hardship brought the crowds onto the streets.

However, hunger alone does not explain revolution. Liberals and nationalists had wanted constitutions and national self-government since 1815, and the Metternich system had blocked every peaceful reform. These middle-class reformers led the revolutions and wrote their demands. The timing was set by Paris: once Louis Philippe fell, news spread quickly and rulers lost their nerve. Britain also suffered hardship but had no revolution, which suggests politics mattered.

Overall economic distress was the main reason why revolution happened in 1848 rather than earlier, because it gave the liberals mass support, but it was the political grievances that gave the revolutions their aims, so it was a necessary cause rather than the only one.

parts.explanation: Both sides and a supported judgement for the top level.

hints: In (b), compare the economic crisis with the political causes and the trigger, then decide.
